title: title, date and argument
short: A carpe diem persuasion printed posthumously in 1681; it argues in three movements: if, but, therefore.
body: The poem was first printed in Miscellaneous Poems (1681), published after Marvell's death; its date of composition is unknown, though the early 1650s is often suggested. It belongs to the Latin carpe diem tradition (Horace, Odes 1.11; Catullus 5, 'Let us live, my Lesbia, and love'). Its three verse paragraphs follow a quasi-syllogism: if we had time (ll. 1-20), but we have not (ll. 21-32), therefore let us love now (ll. 33-46). Eliot, in his 1921 essay, defined Marvell's wit as 'a tough reasonableness' beneath lyric grace and quoted this poem repeatedly in support.

title: coyness
greek: Latin quietus, via Old French coi
short: Reserve, modest shyness, or disdain in love; 'coy' could mean quiet, demure, or affectedly unwilling.
body: From Old French coi (quiet, still), from Latin quietus. In the seventeenth century 'coy' meant modest or shy, often with a hint of coquettish reluctance. The 'crime' of l. 2 is a legal-ethical word that the speaker playfully applies to a courtship delay. The lady's coyness is presented as a social and rhetorical posture, which the speaker undertakes to argue away. The poem's opening concessive ('Had we but ...') grants her virtue full value, but only under impossible conditions.

title: Ganges and Humber
short: The exotic Ganges, with rubies, set against the homely Humber estuary at Hull, Marvell's home town.
body: The Ganges evokes the wealth of India (rubies stand for the jewels of the East). The Humber is the estuary at Hull, where Marvell grew up and which he represented as MP from 1659. The comic disproportion places the lady among jewels and the lover by a muddy northern tide. 'Complain' means to compose love complaints, a lyric genre. The contrast of scale is part of the joke: the world is so large, and time so long, that the lovers could live on opposite sides of it. Hull's link with Marvell gives the line an autobiographical wink.

title: complain
short: To utter a love-complaint, the conventional lament of the rejected lover in Petrarchan verse.
body: The 'complaint' was an established genre in Renaissance poetry (e.g., Daniel's Complaint of Rosamond). The lover will sit by the Humber composing laments, a parody of Petrarchan patience that the poem's argument goes on to reject. Nigel Smith and other editors stress how the first paragraph parodies the patient lover of Petrarchan convention, who waits and laments for years. Placed beside the absurd scale of the courtship that follows, the word marks the lover's patience as a pose that the poem will drop.

title: the Flood and the Conversion of the Jews
short: From Noah's Flood to the conversion of the Jews: the whole span of biblical history up to the end of time.
body: The Flood (Genesis 6-9) was dated in contemporary chronology to around 1656 years after Creation; the conversion of the Jews was expected just before the end of the world (based on Romans 11:25-26), a belief alive among millenarians of the 1650s. The lover would court for all of history and the lady would refuse until its close. The reference to the Jews' conversion had topical point in the 1650s, when millenarian expectation and debates about readmitting Jews to England were current. The hyperbole is precise: the lover would begin before the first great catastrophe and she could refuse until the last.

title: vegetable
short: Growing like a plant, with only the 'vegetative' soul: slow, steady and vast, but not sensual.
body: In Aristotelian psychology the soul had three faculties: vegetative (growth and nutrition, shared with plants), sensitive (animals) and rational (humans). A 'vegetable' love would grow imperceptibly but enormously, 'Vaster then Empires'. Readers have also found a comic, even phallic, undertone in the image of slow growth. 'Then' is the old spelling of 'than'. The adjective thus makes a philosophical joke: the lover pretends his passion could be as patient and unconscious as a growing tree, while the poem's later images reveal its animal energy.

title: the blazon
short: A parody of the Petrarchan blazon, which praises the beloved's body part by part, here measured in centuries.
body: The blazon catalogues the lady's features (eyes, forehead, breasts, 'the rest') in conventional order, assigning absurd stretches of time to each. 'The rest' is a sly euphemism. 'The last Age should show your Heart': only at the end of time would she reveal her feelings. The lover claims she deserves this 'State' (dignity, ceremony) and he would not love at a 'lower rate' (price, valuation).

title: State; rate
short: 'State' means dignified ceremony or high rank; 'rate' means price or value: the language of honour and commerce.
body: These words close the first movement with mock-courtly compliment. 'State' (pomp, dignity) and 'rate' (cost, valuation) prepare for the shift to the economics of time in the second paragraph. The tone of extravagant compliment is sincere only in a conditional world. When the next paragraph begins 'But', these courtly measures are revealed as unaffordable: time, not the lady's merit, sets the true price. 'State' here carries the sense of dignity, ceremony or pomp suited to rank.

title: the turn
short: The second movement begins: the hypothetical of infinite time is replaced by the pressure of mortality.
body: 'But' introduces the minor premise of the argument: we do not have world enough and time. The couplet is among the most quoted in English. The tetrameter couplets continue, but the tone darkens toward the grave. The phrase 'at my back' makes time a pursuer, felt rather than seen. The shift from the conditional mood of the first paragraph to the present indicative ('I alwaies hear') marks the move from fantasy to fact. Eliot quoted the passage in his 1921 essay to show how Marvell's wit can open suddenly onto large imaginative vistas.

title: Time's winged chariot
short: Time as a pursuing charioteer, combining the chariot of the sun with the proverbial idea that time flies (tempus fugit).
body: The image fuses the sun's chariot (Apollo or Phoebus driving across the sky) with Virgil's 'fugit inreparabile tempus' (Georgics 3.284) and emblematic images of winged Time. The lovers are figured as fugitives with the chariot always behind them. The present participle 'hurrying' creates a sense of continuous pursuit. The sound of the line is itself hurried, with 'hurrying' pressing on to the rhyme 'near'.

title: Deserts of vast Eternity
short: Eternity imagined spatially as an endless empty waste, the opposite of the luxurious 'World enough' of the first section.
body: 'Desarts' is the period spelling of deserts, uninhabited wastes. The line reverses the first section: the time once imagined as abundant is now empty and barren. Commentators note the absence of any Christian heaven: eternity is a desolation, an effect that has drawn comment on the poem's secular or libertine stance. 'Yonder all before us' places eternity ahead of the lovers like a landscape stretching to the horizon; the spatial imagination of the first paragraph (Ganges, Humber, empires) returns, but emptied.

title: marble Vault
short: The burial tomb, in which no lover's song will echo; the lady's chastity will be preserved only for worms.
body: The 'marble Vault' is a family tomb. The lover's 'ecchoing Song' will not sound there, and worms will 'try' (test, assay) her long-kept virginity, a grotesque image of violation by death. The macabre wit belongs to the memento mori tradition. The lady's chastity, imagined as long preserved, is mockingly given over to the worms. The lines rework a classical argument for love before death, found in classical epigrams that warn a reluctant girl that no lover will embrace her among the dead.

title: quaint Honour
short: 'Quaint' means fastidious or over-nice, with an obscene pun on Middle English queynte (female genitals); the archive prints 'durst' for 'dust'.
body: 'Quaint' meant ingenious, elaborate, or fastidious; Chaucer's 'queynte' (Miller's Tale) also names the female sex, and most editors accept the pun. 'Honour' here is the lady's chastity. Note that the text in this archive reads 'turn to durst'; the 1681 Folio and standard editions read 'dust', and 'durst' looks like a transcription slip. 'Dust' and 'ashes' recall the burial service ('earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust').

title: the grave
short: Ironic understatement: the tomb is 'fine' and 'private', ideal for love, except that no one embraces there.
body: The couplet's laconic irony is often admired: 'fine' (elegant, exclusive, but also, perhaps, final, from Latin finis) and 'private' are the vocabulary of a lovers' assignation. 'I think' adds a dry, mock-tentative note. Eliot used the couplet to illustrate the alliance of levity and seriousness in Marvell's wit. The rhyme 'place' / 'embrace' pairs the private room of the lovers with the tomb, and the understatement is all the more chilling for its politeness.

title: conclusion
short: The logical conclusion of the syllogism: 'therefore', since time is short, love now.
body: The third paragraph draws the consequence, using the logician's 'therefore'. The repeated 'Now' (ll. 33, 37, 38) drives the rhetoric of urgency, in contrast to the leisured 'would' and 'should' of the opening. Critics have debated how strictly logical the poem is: some see a genuine syllogism, others a parody of logic used for seduction. Either way, 'therefore' marks the speaker's claim that his conclusion follows from the premises he has set out.

title: morning dew / glew
short: The 1681 Folio reads 'glew'; most editors emend to 'dew'; this archive's 'grew' appears to be a slip for 'glew'.
body: This is the poem's best-known textual crux. The Folio prints 'glew'; an early annotated copy (Bodleian MS. Eng. poet. d. 49) corrects it to 'dew', and a manuscript variant (MS. Don b. 8) also reads 'dew'. The OED records 'glew' as an old spelling of 'glow' (and of 'glee'), and some editors defend the Folio reading on that basis; Elizabeth Story Donno's Penguin edition keeps 'glew'. 'Grew' in the archive text is probably a transcription error and has no early authority. Either 'dew' or 'glow' fits the warmth of the next couplet.

title: transpires
short: Breathes out, exhales through the pores of the skin, as fire or vapour: her soul is visibly alight with desire.
body: 'Transpire' is used in its literal sense, to pass out through the pores as vapour (Latin trans + spirare, to breathe). 'Instant' means pressing, urgent, or immediate. The image of the soul exhaling fire through the skin makes desire both physical and spiritual. The lady's body is imagined as a kind of furnace whose inner fire breathes out at every pore. The quasi-scientific vocabulary matches the precise, argumentative language of the rest of the poem.

title: amorous birds of prey
short: Rather than being slowly consumed by Time, the lovers should devour time themselves, as raptors do.
body: The conventional doves of love poetry are replaced by birds of prey. 'Time dev out' in the archive text stands for 'devour' (Folio 'devour'). 'Slow chapt' means slow-jawed (chaps = jaws): Time is imagined as a devourer, the classical Cronos/Saturn eating his children (Ovid's 'tempus edax rerum', Metamorphoses 15.234). Editors note the striking violence of the image after the courtly decorum of the opening; the lover proposes to reverse the relation between lovers and time, making them the predators and time the prey.

title: one Ball
short: The lovers' strength and sweetness rolled into a single sphere: cannonball, pomander, or the sun itself.
body: Editors offer several overlapping senses: a cannonball fired through iron gates (as in a siege), a pomander (a ball of sweet-smelling substances), and a perfect sphere symbolising union, perhaps recalling Plato's androgynes in the Symposium. The 'Iron gates of Life' have been read as the gates of a besieged city, of life itself, and, more bodily, of the womb or virginity. 'Thorough' is the older form of 'through'.

title: Sun stand still
short: Lovers cannot stop the sun, as Joshua did, or as Zeus prolonged a night; they can only make it run faster.
body: In Joshua 10:12-13 the sun stood still at Gibeon; in Greek myth Zeus lengthened the night he spent with Alcmena. The lovers cannot command time like that, but their intensity will make the sun 'run', speeding up time instead of being its victims. Compare Donne's 'The Sun Rising', where the lover also defies the sun; the final couplet turns the poem's opening complaint of too little time into defiant energy.
